availability.notes: Weights (v1.0.0, Hub commit bd7fa122; one classifier and one regressor checkpoint per size: large/medium/small) are public on Hugging Face without gating. Inference runs through NVIDIA's open-source structured-data-models library (Python >= 3.11, PyTorch >= 2.7; GPU strongly recommended, CPU works). As of 2026-09-30 PyPI only holds a placeholder release, so TabArena installs the library from a git pin. The blog states 'Our training recipe and artificial data generators will be released soon' (not available yet). No hosted API; a related NVIDIA NIM exists only for the sibling Kumo Relational model.

architecture.type: column/row interleaved encoder + in-context-learning transformer (TabICLv2 lineage, with TabFM-style Fourier cell embedding)
architecture.parameters_note: Large ≈ 215 M (blog: 'three sizes (28M to 215M parameters)'; checkpoint sizes 854.9 MB classifier / 862.9 MB regressor ≈ 213.7 M / 215.7 M fp32 parameters). Medium ≈ 62 M (246.1 / 250.1 MB ≈ 61.5 M / 62.5 M). Small ≈ 28 M (109.9 / 114.0 MB ≈ 27.5 M / 28.5 M). Exact per-size counts are not published; the estimates come from the .pt file sizes on the Hub.
architecture.layers: Large/Medium: 6 encoder stages (each an induced column block + a row block) + 24 ICL layers; Small: 4 encoder stages + 12 ICL layers (from MODEL_KWARGS in sdm/models/kumo/tabular/model.py)
architecture.embedding_dim: cell/row channels 256 (Large, Medium) or 128 (Small); ICL transformer 1024 (Large) or 512 (Medium, Small) = 4 readout tokens × cell channels, concatenated without projection
architecture.attention_heads: 4 heads in the encoder stages; 16 ICL heads (Large) or 8 (Medium, Small); Test-GQA uses 2 key/value heads for query rows in Medium and Large (none in Small)
architecture.attention_scheme: Encoder: column-wise induced set attention over the rows of each feature group (128 inducing points Small / 256 Medium & Large; context and query cells attend only to context-row keys and values, so cost is linear in rows) interleaved with row-wise attention across a row's feature-group tokens plus 4 learnable readout tokens (rotary positions, theta 100k, to tell columns apart; gated log-scale query scaling). ICL stage: context rows attend to each other, query rows attend to context rows only (each prediction depends only on the context and the row itself), with query-only grouped-query attention ('Test-GQA', 2 KV heads) that shrinks the cache every prediction reads and a reusable context KV cache. All attention blocks use RMSNorm QK-normalisation and a 'length-aware attention temperature': every query is scaled by a temperature growing with log(number of keys), with a coefficient learned per head (LogScale), so attention stays sharp on tables far longer or wider than training tables.
architecture.checkpoints: separate classification and regression checkpoints per size (3 sizes × 2 tasks); library default size = large
architecture.regression_head: distributional: 999 quantiles (q001…q999) via pinball/quantile loss; point prediction = mean over quantiles (after sorting and 20 %-trimmed averaging across estimators); classification head: 10-way class logits (MLP head with GELU, 2× hidden width)
architecture.feature_embedding: Cells are grouped 3 columns per token; numerical and categorical values pass through Fourier features (sines and cosines of 32 learned frequencies) with separate weights per type; missing values are mean-imputed inside the model and flagged through a learned missingness projection (no user-side imputation); every context token also receives a label embedding (class embedding or linear map of the standardised target)
key_innovations: Length-aware attention temperature: per-head learned log-scale query scaling so softmax attention stays sharp when inference tables are much larger than training tables
Test-GQA: query rows use grouped-query attention with 2 KV heads (Medium/Large) and the context KV cache is computed once and reused for follow-up predictions
Interleaved column/row encoder stages (4 or 6) instead of TabICLv2's 3 column + 3 row blocks, with TabFM-style Fourier cell embeddings and a learned missingness channel

Artificial-data generator with built-in real-world imperfections (missingness patterns, coarsened features that make duplicate rows disagree, many-level categoricals, heavy-tailed regression targets) and a tree-ensemble learnability filter
Three sizes (≈28 M / 62 M / 215 M) trained on 35 / 71 / 137 million artificial tables, forming an accuracy–efficiency Pareto front; released under a permissive license (OpenMDW-1.1)

capabilities.max_classes_note: A single forward pass covers up to 10 classes (classification head is 10-wide); the library extends to any number of classes with error-correcting output codes (ECOC, max_classes=10 per sub-problem; code derived from TabPFN-extensions).
capabilities.max_features_note: No hard limit in the model; the default preprocessing recipe keeps at most 500 columns per estimator (SelectColumns(500) after a Latin-square column shuffle, so different estimators see different subsets). Pretraining used up to 100 columns; the blog warns accuracy may degrade 'on tables far beyond the training ranges'.
capabilities.max_samples_note: No hard limit: by default the whole training set is the context (TabArena adapter max_context_size=None; optional --max_context_size subsamples the context into num_estimators chunks). Pretraining contexts reach 60,000 rows (stage 3); column attention is linear in rows, the ICL stage quadratic in context rows. Memory is the practical limit (fp16 autocast on CUDA; estimator batching falls back to one estimator at a time above 3,000 rows or 50,000 cells).
capabilities.categorical_features: numerical and categorical columns only; categoricals are aligned, count-encoded (category counts added for cardinality >= 50) and converted to numbers by the recipe, then embedded with separate categorical Fourier weights. Text, images or timestamps must be turned into features with the library's pre-processing recipes (an examples/tabular/text.py example exists).
capabilities.other: Quantile/uncertainty outputs for regression (999 quantiles); reusable context KV cache (fit once, predict repeatedly); CPU inference supported; fine-tuning example provided (examples/tabular/finetune.py: full fine-tuning of the small model with AdamW, lr 1e-5, cross-entropy or pinball loss). No multi-target and no relational-table support (the sibling Kumo Relational model covers relational data).

pretraining.synthetic_prior_summary: Every training table is sampled from a Structural Causal Model in six steps: (1) draw a whole-table configuration (size, task, mechanisms, missingness); (2) sample a random causal graph over hidden variables; (3) evaluate it root-to-leaf with randomly drawn functions at every node (linear maps, small neural networks, trees, Gaussian processes); (4) turn some nodes into numerical or categorical columns, one into the target, keep the rest hidden (unmeasured causes); (5) post-process: correlate groups of columns, clip outliers, inject missing values; (6) a quick tree-ensemble check discards tables without learnable signal. The generator is a procedural sampler (not a trained model), so it yields an endless supply of tables. Real-world imperfections are built in on purpose: several missingness patterns, coarsened features so duplicate rows may disagree on their label, categorical columns with many levels, heavy-tailed regression targets. Contexts are the labelled majority of rows, the model predicts the remaining rows.
synthetic_prior_types: SCM (random causal DAG over hidden variables)
post-processing: column correlation, outlier clipping, missingness injection, coarsening, many-level categoricals, heavy-tailed targets
pretraining.num_synthetic_datasets_note: 137 million artificial tables for Large; 71 million for Medium; 35 million for Small ('In total, Kumo Tabular-Small/Medium/Large saw about 35/71/137 million artificial tables').
pretraining.objective: cross-entropy for classification; quantile (pinball) loss over 999 fixed quantile levels for regression; classification and regression trained as separate models
pretraining.training_steps: not stated (only the number of tables seen per size)
pretraining.training_cost_note: No GPU type, GPU-hours or cost are published; the blog promises the training recipe 'soon'.
pretraining.curriculum: Three stages as in TabICLv2: stage 1 (longest) tables of 1,024 rows and up to 100 columns; stage 2 varies the context from 400 to 10,240 rows; stage 3 extends the context to 60,000 rows, still with up to 100 columns.

icl.context_note: No fixed window: the entire training table is the context by default. Pretrained on contexts up to 60,000 rows; the length-aware attention temperature is designed to keep attention sharp beyond the training range. Context keys/values can be cached once (fit) and reused for follow-up predictions; query rows are processed in batches.
icl.large_dataset_strategy: Full context by default; optional context subsampling (max_context_size) that gives each of the num_estimators members a random chunk; per-estimator column subsets of at most 500 columns (max_columns override); estimator batching heuristics and fp16 autocast to fit GPU memory; optional KV cache for repeated prediction.
icl.test_time_ensembling: Ensemble of preprocessing members: 16 estimators by default for Large in NVIDIA's TabArena/TALENT adapters (8 for Medium and Small; the model-card example uses num_estimators=8). Members differ by a round-robin choice of numerical transform (identity, power transform, robust scaling + soft clipping, rank-Gaussian), Latin-square column shuffling, categorical level shifts and random target sign flips; class probabilities are averaged before a softmax, regression quantiles are sorted and averaged with a 20 % trimmed mean.
icl.fine_tuning: Supported by the library: examples/tabular/finetune.py does full fine-tuning (AdamW, lr 1e-5, context 256 / query 128 rows per step) of the small model or TabICLv2 with the model's own losses; not used for any reported benchmark number.
icl.inference_notes: Predictions are made in a single forward pass per estimator; each query's prediction depends only on the context and the query row, not on the other queries in the batch. More than 10 classes are handled with error-correcting output codes. Runs under torch.autocast float16 on CUDA in the benchmark adapters.

speed.hardware_note: NVIDIA's TabArena run used a uniform single RTX 6000 Pro setup for all methods; the TabArena maintainers re-run on RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB) spot workers.
speed.memory_note: Not stated. Test-GQA (2 KV heads for queries) and the context KV cache are described as shrinking the per-prediction memory; the adapter batches estimators only while context+query rows <= 3,000 and cells <= 50,000, otherwise one estimator at a time.
speed.speed_claims: 'ranks first overall with an ELO of 1950 while running 17× faster than LimiX-2 under a uniform single RTX 6000 Pro evaluation setup'; all three sizes are claimed to define the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front on TabArena (per-size timings only shown in the blog figure). No absolute seconds-per-1K-rows figures are published; official TabArena timings will follow once PR #625 is merged.
speed.inference_cost_note: Free local inference; no hosted API or pricing.

differences_vs_predecessor: Kumo Tabular is the successor of TabICLv2 by the same lead author (Jingang Qu, now at NVIDIA) and reuses its recipe: column-then-row embedding, ICL transformer, three-stage curriculum, separate classification/regression checkpoints, 999-quantile regression head, Muon-era training tricks are not disclosed. Changes: (1) interleaved column/row encoder stages (4–6) instead of 3 + 3 fixed blocks; (2) TabFM-style Fourier cell embeddings (32 learned frequencies, separate numerical/categorical weights) plus a learned missingness channel instead of TabICLv2's feature embedding; (3) length-aware attention temperature (learned per-head log-scale query scaling) replacing TabICLv2's QASSMax as the mechanism for long contexts; (4) Test-GQA and a reusable context KV cache for cheaper repeated prediction; (5) three model sizes (≈28 M, 62 M, 215 M vs ≈28 M for TabICLv2) trained on 35–137 M tables (vs ≈35 M) with a richer generator (more imperfections); (6) 16 default estimators for Large (TabICLv2: 8); (7) license OpenMDW-1.1 (TabICLv2: BSD-3-Clause); the generator and training code are not yet public (TabICLv2's are).
